stem: The pathophysiology of ischemic nephropathy is primarily due to:
options: Obstructive nephropathy
Isolated thickening of basement membrane
Chronic hypoperfusion
Acute renal artery occlusion
Decreased filtering in the loop of Henle

stem: A 73-year-old man is referred for recalcitrant hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Blood pressure is 180/95, despite a 4-drug regimen. Renal duplex notes an atrophic right kidney and peak systolic velocities of 220 cm/s through the proximal left main renal artery. The next best step in the management of this patient is:
options: Diagnostic arteriogram
Computed tomography arteriogram (CTA)
Magnetic resonance arteriogram (MRA)
Captopril scintigraphy
Renal biopsy

stem: A 63-year-old woman with uncontrolled hypertension on two medications undergoes MR angiography to evaluate for renal artery stenosis, interpreted as an indeterminant stenosis of the left renal artery. A significant limitation of renal artery imaging by MR angiography:
options: Delivers more ionizing radiation to the patient than CT imaging
Has higher contrast requirements than CT imaging
More susceptible to respiratory movement of the kidney and can overestimate stenosis
Heavy ostial calcification makes it difficult to quantify stenoses
Is unable to detect small distal renal artery variations

stem: A 62-year-old man with high-grade renal stenosis is undergoing angiography prior to endovascular imaging. The technique recommended to improve imaging quality during renal artery angiography is:
options: Placement of the patient’s arm tucked by the patient’s side and use of steep oblique (>60%) imaging
Instructing the patient to take multiple deep breaths during the contrast injection
Large volume contrast injection through an end hole catheter directed towards the side of the stenosis
Using a non-subtracted image mode with placement of a flush catheter just above the renal arteries
Decreasing the frame rate to a low frame mode such as 2 frames/sec

stem: A 65-year-old man with hypertension who has been on angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor for the past 6 months presents with worsening renal dysfunction and a serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL. Examination demonstrates an abdominal bruit. Renal artery duplex demonstrates a right renal artery peak systolic velocity (PSV) of 220 cm/sec and left renal artery PSV of 230 cm/sec. The most likely cause of his worsening renal function is:
options: Renal artery dissection
Bilateral renal artery stenosis
Takayasu arteritis
Left renal artery stenosis
ACE inhibitor toxicity

stem: A 72-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction of 35%) and a single left kidney undergoes endovascular aneurysm repair for a 6.4-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. During the procedure the left renal artery is inadvertently covered. Attempts at endovascular salvage are unsuccessful. The next most appropriate step in management is:
options: Iliorenal bypass
Splenorenal bypass
Hepatorenal bypass
Aortorenal bypass from the supra-celiac aorta
Renal auto-transplantation

stem: A 55-year-old man with bilateral atherosclerotic ostial renal artery stenosis and hypertension managed with 4 medications, presents for surgical consultation. He has no significant cardiovascular comorbidity. He has single renal arteries bilaterally, no notable celiac or superior mesenteric arterial disease, and a normal caliber aorta without transmural calcification. The most appropriate surgical option for revascularization is:
options: Transaortic aortorenal thrombendarterectomy via a transverse incision
Bilateral aortorenal bypass with hypogastric arterial conduit
Direct aortic reimplantation of bilateral renal arteries
Extra-anatomic renal artery bypass
Ex-vivo renal artery revascularization

stem: Both the Angioplasty and Stenting for Renal Artery Lesions (ASTRAL) and the Cardiovascular in Renal Atherosclerotic Lesions (CORAL) trials reported outcomes for renal artery stenting for renovascular hypertension. The statement that is most consistent with those outcomes is:
options: Artery stenting is only beneficial for blood pressure reduction in female patients
Artery stenting is not medically necessary in patients with adequate blood pressure control and stable renal function
Artery stenting is more likely to prevent the need for hemodialysis than in patients without intervention
Artery stenting is associated with better long-term blood pressure control than medical treatment alone
Artery stenting is likely to result in a pooled decrease in death, stroke, and myocardial infarction compared to patients receiving medications alone.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with evidence of bilateral atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis and a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR). The following factor has been shown to be most important in predicting preservation of renal function if renal angioplasty and stenting is performed in this setting:
options: Degree of stenosis of the renal arteries to be treated
Preprocedural degree of renal dysfunction as measured by GFR
Patient age
Preprocedural blood pressure control
Number of preprocedural anti-hypertensive agents patient requires

stem: A 68-year-old man is incidentally noted to have a 70% right renal artery stenosis on an otherwise negative CT scan performed for evaluation of abdominal pain that has now resolved. He is referred to vascular surgery for evaluation and potential intervention. He is taking 1 anti-hypertensive medication with a blood pressure of 130/70 mm Hg and a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL. The best management of this patient is:
options: No intervention and annual CT angiography surveillance but no intervention
Angioplasty and stenting of the lesion as a potential first line therapy rather than the initiation of blood pressure medication if needed
No intervention is required
Intervention in the absence of congestive heart failure or flash pulmonary edema
Catheter-based angiography to verify the CT findings

stem: A 77-year-old woman presents with an incidentally discovered 2-cm main renal artery aneurysm (RAA). She is otherwise healthy without hypertension. The most appropriate option for management is:
options: Aneurysm excision with primary re-anastomosis
Endovascular exclusion of the renal aneurysm with a covered stent
Routine surveillance with annual MR angiogram
Aneurysm repair via ex-vivo reconstruction

stem: The diagnosis of renal vein thrombosis in a non-transplanted patient is most accurately determined by:
options: Color Doppler
MRI
CT with intravenous contrast
Intravenous urogram
Catheter venography

stem: Initial management of renal vein thrombosis is:
options: Anticoagulation
Intra-arterial thrombolysis
Intravenous thrombolysis
Nephrectomy
Operative thrombectomy

stem: A 45-year-old man with no prior history of hypertension presents with severe uncontrolled right flank pain and hematuria. His right arm blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. A computed tomographic angiography of the abdomen demonstrates an isolated right renal artery dissection with extension into the branch vessels and cortical infarction. Renal artery angiogram shows arterial dissection into the cortical branches. The optimal treatment for this patient is:
options: Renal artery angioplasty with a drug coated balloon.
Renal artery balloon expandable stent placement
Right nephrectomy
Renal artery bypass with PTFE
Observation and initiating antihypertensive medication

stem: A 39-year-old man is evaluated after a new onset of renal insufficiency and hypertension following a renal biopsy for a suspicious mass on the kidney. On examination, his abdomen is soft with a bruit on the left flank and noticeable varicoceles on the scrotum. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Renal carcinoma
Arteriovenous malformation
Diabetic nephropathy
Renal arteriovenous fistula (AVF)
May-Thurner syndrome

stem: A 42-year-old patient with a renal transplant undergoes a transplant biopsy due to worsening renal function. Three months later, a renal duplex is performed for persistent decline in renal function. The transplant renal duplex reveals an arteriovenous fistula (AVF). An indication for intervention is:
options: Persistent hypertension, even if controlled with medication
Intermittent microscopic hematuria, that does not require transfusion
Persistence at 9 months, even without symptoms
Intermittent lumbar pain, controlled with oral analgesics
Persistent worsening creatinine

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent hematuria and flank pain. On physical examination, she has a right abdominal bruit. A duplex ultrasound is ordered. The duplex finding that is most consistent with a renal arteriovenous malformation is:
options: Decreased peak systolic velocity with low end-diastolic flow
Decreased peak systolic velocity with high end-diastolic flow
Increased peak systolic velocity with low end diastolic flow
Increased peak systolic velocity with high end diastolic flow
Increased peak systolic velocity with reversal of diastolic flow

stem: A 38-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed right renal congenital arteriovenous malformation is referred for possible intervention due to recurrent episodes of hematuria requiring blood transfusions. The most appropriate technique for endovascular treatment of renal arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) is:
options: Gelatin sponge is best used in the treatment of smaller AVMs
Direct puncture with alcohol injection
Micro-coils are favored over glues and alcohols
Large AVMs should initially be treated by radiofrequency ablation
Covered stents should not be used to treat AVMs

stem: The key visceral artery involved in chronic mesenteric ischemia is:
options: Inferior mesenteric artery
Superior mesenteric artery
Gastroduodenal artery
Celiac artery
Arc of Riolan

stem: A key historic factor in a patient presenting with acute mesenteric ischemia due to an embolic event would be:
options: Atrial fibrillation
Diabetes
Peripheral arterial disease
Hypertension
Hypercoagulability

stem: A 75-year-old woman has a 6-month history of weight loss and recent post-prandial abdominal pain with food fear. A mesenteric arterial duplex demonstrates severe stenosis of the celiac artery, focal occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and a patent inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) without stenosis. The main collateral pathway that is providing blood flow to the SMA is:
options: Gastroduodenal artery
Pancreaticoduodenal artery
Hemorrhoidal branches from the internal iliac artery
Epigastric artery
Arc of Riolan

stem: A 21-year-old lean woman presents with painless post-prandial bilious emesis after intentionally losing 20 pounds. Gastrointestinal work up has ruled out intrinsic gastric pathology, a motility disorder, as well as an eating disorder. Despite aggressive work up, the patient continues to lose weight and has a nasojejunal tube placed which allows her to begin to gain weight. The anatomic finding that is the most likely cause of her symptoms is:
options: Superior mesenteric artery critical stenosis
J-hook configuration of the celiac artery
Replaced right hepatic artery
Narrowed aorto-mesenteric angle
Left renal vein stenosis

stem: An 85-year-old woman with history of atrial fibrillation held her anticoagulation for one week for a dental procedure. She now presents to the emergency department with acute onset of abdominal pain. Her laboratory panel demonstrates moderate leukocytosis and a high anion gap acidosis. The next step in determining the diagnosis for this patient is:
options: Abdominal plain radiograph
Mesenteric duplex ultrasonography
Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)
CT angiography (CTA)
Diagnostic laparoscopy

stem: A duplex ultrasound is ordered to evaluate a 59-year-old woman with chronic abdominal pain. The duplex criterion that would be suggestive of a diagnosis of chronic mesenteric ischemia is:
options: A peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the celiac artery of 190 cm/sec and in the superior mesenteric artery of 260 cm/sec
A PSV in the celiac artery of 210 cm/sec and in the superior mesenteric artery of 260 cm/sec
Retrograde flow in the hepatic and splenic artery with a superior mesenteric artery PSV of 260 cm/sec
Retrograde flow in the hepatic and splenic artery with a superior mesenteric artery PSV of 290 cm/sec
Heavy shadowing of the celiac and superior mesenteric artery origin with an elevated end diastolic velocity (EDV) of 43 cm/seconds.

stem: The key imaging angle for the origin of the superior mesenteric artery is:
options: Anteroposterior
Posteroanterior
Right anterior oblique
Left anterior oblique
Lateral

stem: For endovascular management of an orificial lesion of the superior mesenteric artery, proper stent placement would be:
options: Immediately flush with the edge of the aorta
3 mm beyond the origin of the superior mesenteric artery to avoid encroaching upon the aorta
Centered over the lesion but not extending into the aorta
Covering the lesion while extending several mm into the aorta
Extending at least one cm into the aorta

stem: An 85-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation held her anticoagulation for 1 week for a dental procedure. She now presents to the emergency department with acute onset of severe abdominal pain. Her laboratory panel demonstrates moderate leukocytosis and a high anion gap acidosis. A CT angiogram shows an embolus to the proximal portion of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). The most appropriate management is:
options: Retrograde SMA bypass from the left common iliac artery
Embolectomy via a transverse SMA arteriotomy
Embolectomy via a longitudinal SMA arteriotomy
Mesenteric angiography with SMA stent placement
Antegrade SMA bypass using synthetic graft

stem: A 75-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and compensated congestive heart failure has a 1-month history of weight loss and recently has had food fear with abdominal pain. She had a prior superior mesenteric artery (SMA) stent placement 6 weeks ago. CT angiography demonstrates severe stenosis of the celiac artery, occlusion of a stent at the SMA and stenosis of the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). There is minimal calcification at the bilateral common iliac arteries. Of the following, the most appropriate next step for this patient is:
options: Mechanical thrombolysis with balloon angioplasty of the SMA
Antegrade prosthetic bypass to the celiac and IMA
Retrograde prosthetic bypass from the left common iliac artery to the SMA
Retrograde prosthetic bypass from the right internal iliac artery to the SMA and IMA
Open thrombectomy of the SMA

stem: A 12-year-old girl who had recent spine surgery was recently diagnosed with superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome. The most appropriate treatment initial option for this patient is:
options: Naso-jejunal feeding tube
Total parenteral nutrition (TPN)
Division of the ligament of Treitz
Duodenojejunostomy
Aorto-SMA bypass

stem: A 75-year-old man with a history of endocarditis presents with increasing abdominal pain, low-grade fever, 15-lb weight loss, and nausea. His abdomen is tender but there is no guarding. A CT angiography demonstrates a 3-cm superior mesenteric artery (SMA) aneurysm with associated inflammation. Antibiotics are initiated. The most appropriate next step for this patient is:
options: Aneurysmectomy with interposition greater saphenous vein bypass
Antegrade SMA bypass with prosthetic
Endovascular covered stent placement
Ligation of the SMA
Retrograde prosthetic bypass from the left common iliac artery to the SMA

stem: Upon arrival to the recovery room following coil embolization of a 3-cm splenic artery aneurysm, the patient complains of left flank pain and pleuritic chest pain. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Splenic rupture
Splenic infarction
Pancreatitis
Retroperitoneal hematoma
Myocardial infarction

stem: A 61-year-old woman presents with persistently symptomatic uterine fibroids that failed conservative management. The most appropriate management is:
options: Surgical hysterectomy
Uterine artery embolization for fibroids <5 cm in maximum dimension
Uterine artery embolization with administration of embolic agents to the bilateral uterine arteries
Uterine myomectomy to include the fibroid
Surgical ligation of the bilateral uterine arteries

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with pelvic pain, flank pain, and hematuria. The CT finding most consistent with an etiology for these symptoms is:
options: Widening of the left renal vein at the aortomesenteric portion
Right ovarian vein drainage into the inferior vena cava
Decreased angle between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta (less than 40 degrees)
Non-visualization of the left ovarian vein
The presence of a horseshoe kidney

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents with severe post-chemotherapeutic thrombocytopenia related to autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Past medical history includes multiple abdominal operations for ischemic bowel during treatment of her malignancy and the presence of a stoma. The most appropriate role for splenic artery embolization in this case is:
options: There is no role for splenic artery embolization in this case
Preoperative splenic artery embolization should be performed in preparation for splenectomy
Splenic embolization can be performed as a primary therapy with the goal of complete hematologic response of her autoimmune hemolytic anemia
Splenic artery embolization should be performed only if liquid embolization agents are available
Splenic artery embolization should be performed as a test to determine if the thrombocytopenia is autoimmune in origin

stem: A 64-year-old patient with acute mesenteric ischemia from a cardiac embolic source is taken to the operating room for an embolectomy of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). Exposure of the SMA is accomplished by:
options: Mobilizing the spleen and splenic flexure of the left colon and rotating the viscera towards the patient’s right (medial visceral rotation)
Mobilizing the proximal duodenum and pancreatic head toward the patient’s left (Kocher maneuver)
Identification of a jejunal branch of the SMA in the small bowel mesentery and performing a retrograde thrombectomy
Elevation of the transverse mesocolon and rotating the small bowel toward the patient’s right and identification of the SMA at the inferior pancreatic border
Mobilization of the gastrohepatic ligament and inferior retraction of the stomach

stem: A 38-year-old moderately obese man presents to the emergency room with worsening abdominal pain over the last week. The patient’s past medical history is significant for factor V Leiden mutation identified due to a family history of deep venous thrombosis. His laboratory data and plain x-rays are negative. A diagnosis of mesenteric venous thrombosis is considered. The optimal imaging study for this patient is:
options: Duplex ultrasonography
CT scan with intravenous and oral contrast
CT scan with intravenous contrast and imaging in the portal venous phase
Arteriogram of the superior mesenteric artery with delayed imaging
Diagnostic laparoscopy with identification of dilated and congested appearing bowel

stem: A 38-year-old man was involved in a motor vehicle crash 8 hours ago. He is hemodynamically stable and his injuries include multiple rib fractures, a grade 2 liver injury, pneumothorax, and non-enhancement of his left kidney on CT scan consistent with intimal left renal artery injury. The most appropriate next step in his management is:
options: Treatment of other injuries as necessary and non-operative management of his left renal artery injury
Immediate exploratory laparotomy and open thrombectomy and repair of the left renal artery
Arteriogram and endovascular treatment of the left renal artery
Exploratory laparotomy and aortorenal bypass of the renal artery
Exploratory laparotomy and nephrectomy

stem: A 32-year-old man was involved in a high-speed motorcycle crash and has a pelvic fracture and CT scan reveals a pelvic hematoma with contrast extravasation from a branch of the internal iliac artery. The most appropriate next step in the management of this patient is:
options: Proceed to the operating room with exploration of the pelvic hematoma
Orthopedic fixation of the fracture and observation of the patient in the intensive care unit
Arteriogram and identification and embolization of the bleeding vessel
Attempt at CT-guided embolization of the bleeding vessel
Arteriogram and coil embolization of the proximal internal iliac artery

stem: A 42-year-old woman with symptomatic nutcracker syndrome underwent a left renal vein angioplasty and stent. The following is a potential adverse outcome or consequence with this procedure:
options: Need for anticoagulation
Need for dual antiplatelet therapy
Poor patency
Reduction in renal-caval pressure gradient
Risk of stent fracture
